article.overview: A high-resolution camera records images in which features at metre to sub-metre scale can be distinguished on a planetary surface. For the Moon, such cameras have been flown in lunar orbit. They are built around a long-focal-length telescope and a fine-pitch detector. A fine ground sample needs a narrow field of view, so each image covers only a few kilometres and mapping a large area takes many orbits. This article describes the generic class and three flown lunar orbital examples: the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera Narrow Angle Camera (NAC), the ShadowCam instrument on the Korea Pathfinder Lunar Orbiter (KPLO, Danuri), and the Orbiter High Resolution Camera (OHRC) on Chandrayaan-2 [1][2][3][4][5][6].
article.description:
A high-resolution camera is usually a telescope that focuses light onto a linear or area detector. For a given altitude, the ground size of one detector pixel depends on the telescope's focal length and the angular size of the pixel, as described under Operating Principle. The examples in this article are line-scanning instruments. As the spacecraft moves, a single detector line sweeps across the surface, and the successive lines are assembled into an image. The LROC NAC is a monochrome push-broom scanner [1].

Two of the examples, ShadowCam and OHRC, use time delay integration (TDI). In a TDI sensor, the charge generated by a scene is shifted along the detector in step with the image motion, so that the same ground point is integrated over several successive lines. This increases the collected signal, which matters in dim light [4][6]. The ShadowCam sensor operates across six channels [4]. OHRC offers 64, 128, 192 or 256 TDI stages [6].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
High-resolution images are used to examine small craters, boulders, regolith textures, layering and recent impact sites, and to build high-resolution maps and digital elevation models. The LROC factsheet lists eight original measurement objectives, including finding potential landing sites, mapping regions of permanent shadow or illumination, creating high-resolution maps of polar massifs, deriving high-resolution topography from multi-angle observations, and determining impact hazards [2]. These are mission objectives rather than results, and they are cited only to show application areas.

ShadowCam is designed to image the interiors of permanently shadowed regions (PSRs). The ShadowCam archive states that it focuses on PSRs larger than 10 km at a nominal pixel scale of 1.7 m [4]. OHRC's primary goal was to image a landing-site region before landing, for surface characterisation and the identification of hazard-free zones. Its authors describe generating a digital elevation model and a hazard map from these images [6].
article.operating_principle:
In a simple model, the ground size of one pixel equals the altitude multiplied by the instantaneous field of view (IFOV), which is the angle subtended by one detector pixel. The LROC NAC has an IFOV of 10 microradians, which gives 0.5 m per pixel from the nominal 50 km orbit (arithmetic: 50 km x 10 microradians = 0.5 m) [1][2]. A finer ground sample therefore needs a smaller IFOV, a lower altitude, or both. For OHRC, the authors give a nadir ground sampling distance of 0.25 m from 100 km altitude [6].

The LROC NAC uses a 700 mm focal-length telescope whose image falls on a 5000-pixel CCD line array in each camera [1]. The line is read out as the spacecraft moves, so the scene is built up line by line [1]. The NAC data are sampled to 12 bits and then companded to 8 bits before a lossless compression step prior to downlink [1].

The ShadowCam TDI sensor has six channels. Each channel has two lead-in pixels, eight bias pixels, 512 scene pixels and two lead-out pixels, giving a raw image width of 3,144 pixels and a 3,072-pixel scene width [4]. The bias pixels are shielded from light and are used for calibration [4]. The ShadowCam telescope design follows the LROC NAC, with modifications to reduce stray light [4].

OHRC combines large focal-length optics, a small-pixel detector and TDI to achieve high spatial resolution while keeping a usable signal-to-noise ratio at low illumination [6]. Its imaging depends on the TDI stage selected, the integration time, the roll and pitch angles and the Sun elevation angle [6].
article.scientific_importance: A high-resolution camera turns orbital observations into measurements of features a few metres or less across. The LROC NAC has been in lunar orbit since 2009 and returns 0.5 m panchromatic images over a 5 km swath at 50 km altitude [2]. ShadowCam is intended to image the interiors of PSRs, which receive no direct sunlight. Its authors report a sensitivity 205 times that of the LROC NAC and a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 100 over a large part of its dynamic range [3]. The archive describes a specialised requirement for high sensitivity to image the PSRs [4]. OHRC's authors describe the instrument as the highest spatial resolution camera ever flown in lunar orbit. That is the authors' own statement, which was not independently checked here [6]. ISRO's public summary gives the resolution as about 30 cm [5].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a high-resolution camera. The three examples below use different orbits, telescope designs, detectors and operating modes, so their values are not directly comparable and no comparison table is given. Each value is tied to the named instrument and its source. Where a value was not found in the sources read, it is recorded as null rather than estimated.

examples.name: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera Narrow Angle Camera (NAC)
examples.type: Flown lunar orbital instrument (one of two NAC units on LRO)
examples.status: flown; in lunar orbit since 2009 (LROC factsheet)
examples.pixel_scale_note: nominal at 50 km altitude (asterisked in factsheet)
examples.detector: Kodak KLI-5001G; factsheet pixel format 1 x 5,064; Robinson et al. describe a 5000-pixel CCD line array
examples.volume_note: 70 cm x 27 cm diameter, as listed in the LROC factsheet
examples.notes:
The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter carries two Narrow Angle Cameras, NAC-Left and NAC-Right [1][2]. Each is a monochrome push-broom scanner with a 700 mm focal-length telescope and a 2.85 degree cross-track field of view. Together they cover a 5 km swath at 50 km altitude [1][2]. The factsheet lists an effective focal length of 700 mm, an f/3.59 Cassegrain (Ritchey-Chretien) optical design, a 195 mm primary mirror diameter, a Kodak KLI-5001G detector with a 1 x 5,064 pixel format, and a 400-750 nm sensitivity range [2]. The factsheet's pixel scale of 0.5 m and its image-size values are marked with an asterisk, which the factsheet ties to an altitude of 50 km [2]. Robinson et al. describe a 5000-pixel CCD line array [1], so the factsheet pixel-format figure and the paper's description differ slightly. Both are recorded as published.

The factsheet gives per-NAC engineering values of 8.2 kg mass, a volume listed as 70 cm x 27 cm diameter, a peak power of 9.3 W, an average power of 6.4 W and a 28 V DC supply [2]. The factsheet's table columns were extracted from a multi-column PDF, so these assignments should be checked against the scanned page before reuse. Detailed NAC treatment belongs to payload 045 (Narrow-angle camera) and is not repeated here.

examples.name: ShadowCam (KPLO / Danuri)
examples.type: Flown lunar orbital instrument (NASA-provided camera on a KARI spacecraft)
examples.status: flown on KPLO (Danuri), as described by the ShadowCam archive and calibration paper
examples.pixel_scale_note: nominal, per ShadowCam archive and calibration paper
examples.snr_note: greater than 100 over a large part of the dynamic range (calibration paper abstract)
examples.host: Korea Pathfinder Lunar Orbiter (KPLO, Danuri), flown by KARI
examples.notes:
ShadowCam is a panchromatic camera flown on the Korea Pathfinder Lunar Orbiter (KPLO, Danuri), a mission of the Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI) [3][4]. The calibration paper describes it as a NASA-provided camera for the KPLO mission [3]. Its telescope design is based on the LROC NAC, with modifications for stray-light reduction [4]. The nominal pixel scale is 1.7 m [3][4]. The archive describes the sensor as a TDI device with six channels, each with 512 scene pixels, two lead-in and two lead-out pixels and eight bias pixels, giving a 3,072-pixel scene width [4].

The calibration paper reports a sensitivity 205 times that of the LROC NAC and a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 100 over a large part of the dynamic range. It also reports an optical performance that supports the full 1.7 m image scale [3]. The paper states that stray light is a major challenge and that very bright terrain in or near the field of view produces artefacts [3]. These values come from the calibration paper abstract, which is the only part of that paper read for this article [3].

Focal length, aperture, mass, power and dimensions are not stated in the sources read for this article [3][4]. A search summary of the ShadowCam factsheet mentioned some values, but the factsheet could not be retrieved at the time of checking, so those values are not used here.

examples.name: Orbiter High Resolution Camera (OHRC), Chandrayaan-2
examples.type: Flown lunar orbital instrument (ISRO orbiter payload)
examples.status: flown; Chandrayaan-2 orbiter in lunar orbit from 2019 (IAF 2020 paper)
examples.gsd_note: nadir ground sampling distance as stated in IAF 2020 paper; ISRO public summary gives about 30 cm
examples.snr_note: SNR 70 at 128 TDI at reference radiance about 0.5 mW/(cm2.sr.m), per IAF 2020 paper
examples.orbit_history: launch 22 July 2019; lunar orbit insertion 20 August 2019; 119 km x 127 km orbit reached 1 September 2019; perilune trimmed to about 95 km for OHRC operations
examples.notes:
The OHRC is the high-resolution camera on the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter [5][6]. The integrated orbiter and lander module was launched on 22 July 2019, entered lunar orbit on 20 August 2019 as a composite module, and reached a 119 km x 127 km orbit on 1 September 2019. Orbit-trimming manoeuvres then achieved a perilune of about 95 km for OHRC imaging over the south-polar landing-site region [6].

The IAF paper gives a nadir ground sampling distance of 0.25 m and a nadir swath of 3 km from 100 km altitude, in the panchromatic band of 450-800 nm [6]. OHRC uses TDI with 64, 128, 192 or 256 stages. The paper gives an SNR of 70 at 128 TDI stages at a reference radiance of about 0.5 mW/(cm2.sr.m) [6]. The instrument can provide stereoscopic views in consecutive orbits by spacecraft manoeuvre, for digital elevation model generation [6].

ISRO's public summary describes OHRC as giving the highest-resolution optical images ever (about 30 cm) from a lunar orbiter [5]. The 0.25 m nadir ground sampling distance in the IAF paper and the approximately 30 cm public figure are not reconciled in the sources read. Mass, power and dimensions for OHRC are not stated in the sources read and are recorded as null.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions and proportions. Only the LRO NAC has a published dimension in the sources read: its volume is listed as 70 cm x 27 cm diameter per camera [2]. Dimensions for ShadowCam and OHRC are not stated in the sources read and are recorded as null. A new high-resolution camera's dimensions would depend on its telescope length, baffle and radiator design, and on the host spacecraft's mounting envelope.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass and weight. The LRO NAC is listed at 8.2 kg per camera [2]. The Robinson et al. NAC section read for this article does not give a separate mass figure [1]. ShadowCam and OHRC mass values are not stated in the sources read and are recorded as null.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power requirements. The LRO NAC is listed with a peak power of 9.3 W, an average power of 6.4 W and a 28 V DC supply [2]. ShadowCam and OHRC power values are not stated in the sources read and are recorded as null. Power figures for the examples are per-instrument values and should not be compared with spacecraft-level power budgets.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
Orbital high-resolution cameras operate in the lunar orbital thermal environment. Robinson et al. identify the combination of near diffraction-limited performance at a half-metre ground sample distance, a wide field, the orbital thermal environment and low mass as the principal challenges of the NAC optical design [1].

Image geometry and illumination are operational constraints. OHRC operations were planned around the TDI stage, integration time, roll and pitch angles, orbit parameters and Sun elevation angle [6]. For PSR imaging, ShadowCam must work in very dark conditions and control stray-light artefacts from bright terrain in or near its field of view [3][4].

Data handling is also a constraint. Each LROC NAC buffers 256 MB of uncompressed data, enough for a full-swath image 25 km long or a 2x-binned image 104 km long, before lossless compression for downlink [1].
article.limitations:
The swath is narrow. The LRO NAC pair covers 5 km at 50 km altitude [2], and OHRC's nadir swath is 3 km at 100 km [6]. Covering a large region at this resolution therefore requires many orbits or targeted imaging. This is an inference from the swath values, not a measured operational figure.

Published resolution values are not always consistent. The IAF paper gives an OHRC nadir ground sampling distance of 0.25 m [6], while ISRO's public summary gives about 30 cm [5]. The LRO NAC pixel scale is a nominal value at 50 km altitude [2].

Stray light and bright-terrain artefacts limit imaging of dark regions. The calibration paper reports them as a major challenge for ShadowCam [3].

Several engineering values could not be verified in the sources read: the ShadowCam focal length, aperture, mass, power and dimensions, and the OHRC mass, power and dimensions [3][4][6]. These are recorded as null in the JSON.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: All three examples are orbital instruments. Their integration path is spacecraft integration, launch, transfer to lunar orbit, orbit insertion and trimming, commissioning and operation. No surface deployment of any of the three is described in the sources read.
transportation_process: Integrate the camera into the orbiter, with its pointing, thermal and data interfaces defined by the host spacecraft.
Launch the spacecraft and transfer it toward the Moon. For OHRC, the integrated module was launched on 22 July 2019 and entered lunar orbit on 20 August 2019 [6].

Insert into lunar orbit and trim the orbit to the required altitude or perilune. For OHRC, the module reached a 119 km x 127 km orbit and was trimmed to a perilune of about 95 km for imaging operations [6].
Commission the instrument, including calibration of the sensors and actuators, which the OHRC paper describes as part of the early mission sequence [6].

Operate the camera with attitude control and detector settings chosen for the illumination geometry. For OHRC, these include the TDI stage, integration time, roll and pitch angles and Sun elevation [6]. The LRO NAC buffers image data before downlink [1].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Surface deployment is not applicable to these examples. The cameras are fixed to orbiter structures. Imaging is achieved by push-broom scanning [1] or TDI scanning [4][6], together with spacecraft attitude control. The OHRC stereo capability uses spacecraft manoeuvres in consecutive orbits [6].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The LRO has carried the LROC NAC pair since 2009 [2]. The KPLO mission carries ShadowCam [3][4]. Chandrayaan-2 carried OHRC, which reached its operating orbit in 2019 [6]. No surface-deployed high-resolution camera example is verified in this run.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is asserted for any example beyond the host spacecraft named in the sources. A surface-mounted high-resolution camera would need verified interfaces for mass, power, mounting, pointing, thermal control and data before any lander assessment. None of these interfaces is verified here.

article.historical_significance:
The LROC NAC has been in lunar orbit since 2009 and provides 0.5 m panchromatic images [2]. Its telescope design was the basis for ShadowCam [4]. The ShadowCam archive describes the instrument as designed to capture panchromatic high-resolution images inside PSRs for the first time, building on NAC heritage [4]. The calibration paper gives its sensitivity relative to the NAC [3].

OHRC, flown on Chandrayaan-2, is described by its operations paper as the highest spatial resolution camera ever flown in lunar orbit. That is an authors' statement [6]. These three examples illustrate successive lunar high-resolution imaging systems in orbit. The sources read do not give a full history of the class, and earlier lunar orbiter camera systems and Chang'e-series cameras were not reviewed in this run.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The payload name 'High-resolution camera' describes a class of instruments rather than one design. The three examples differ in orbit, optics, detector technique and operating mode, and their values must not be combined or compared as if they described one instrument. The NAC values come from the LROC factsheet and from the overview and NAC sections of Robinson et al. (2010) read in this run. The ShadowCam values come from the calibration paper abstract and the PDS archive specification, and the calibration paper and factsheet were not read in full. The OHRC values come from the 2020 IAF operations paper and ISRO's public summary. Several values are unverified and recorded as null. No image asset was verified, so the article contains no embedded images. Chang'e-series and other national high-resolution cameras were not included because primary specifications were not obtained in this run. The Chang'e-2 stereo CCD camera is covered by payload 029 (Stereo camera), and terrain mapping cameras are covered by payload 028 (Terrain mapping camera).

data_quality_notes: No direct image asset was verified in this run. The image registry is empty, no image is embedded in the Markdown, and no image_url is recorded. Official image pages for the LROC NAC, ShadowCam and OHRC were not located with verifiable direct asset URLs.

OHRC mass, power and dimensions are not stated in the sources read and are null.

The Humm et al. (2023) calibration paper was read from its abstract only. Robinson et al. (2010) was read for its overview and NAC sections only. The ShadowCam archive was read for sections 1-5 only.
